title: Terminal cleaning after a patient leaves
audience: Cleaning staff who clean rooms and bed spaces after discharge or transfer in hospitals and other healthcare settings.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish routine, scheduled and terminal cleaning.
Sequence a terminal clean from linen and waste removal through to the final check.
Explain why detergent comes before disinfectant on high-touch items after discharge.

instruction.heading: What terminal cleaning is for
instruction.body: After a patient departs a room, the space is not simply tidied for the next arrival. The source separates three kinds of cleaning. Routine cleaning keeps the patient zone free of organic matter while someone is staying there. Scheduled cleaning deals with dust and soil on surfaces that people do not usually touch. Terminal cleaning follows discharge or transfer, reaches the immediate patient space and the surrounding care area, and aims to strip out organic material and cut microbial contamination so that none passes on to the next occupant. Treat it as its own task with its own checklist, not as a longer routine clean.

instruction.heading: Sequencing the work
instruction.body: Begin only when the discharge is confirmed and the people who own the equipment have removed it or cleared it. Remove and bag linen and waste first, following “Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling” and “Soiled and clean linen: handling and storage”. Work from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest, and from the ceiling downward, so that debris does not fall onto surfaces already cleaned. Clean high-touch items such as bed rails, call bells, switches, door handles, taps and over-bed tables with detergent first, because organic material can block a disinfectant from reaching the surface, as “Detergent first: physical cleaning before any disinfectant” explains.

instruction.heading: Disinfection and drying
instruction.body: Apply disinfectant only where the risk review or the item's frequency table requires it, using a product on the approved list under “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals”. Keep the surface wet for the product's contact time before you wipe, and allow it to air dry instead of wiping it early. The source describes heavier methods for outbreaks and specialised areas. Those are covered in “Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread” and are not repeated here, and no product concentration or dosing from the source is used in this lesson.

procedure: Check the discharge notice or work order and confirm the room is clear of the patient and their equipment.
Gather the terminal cleaning checklist and the approved products for the room's risk level.
Remove linen and waste into the correct containers, following “Clinical waste: segregation, containers and handling” and “Soiled and clean linen: handling and storage”.
Clean the high-touch items with detergent first, starting furthest from the door.
Clean the floor and the wider care surfaces, moving from the cleanest spot to the dirtiest and from high points to low.
Apply the approved disinfectant only where the schedule requires it, observe the contact time, and let the surface dry.
Log the room and any item you could not clean, then report the room as ready once the check is complete.

workedExamples.situation: A bed space in a 28-bed general ward is free after a patient moves to theatre. The bed frame and bedside table have a small smear of blood on them.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the order of work, and how is the blood handled?
workedExamples.reasoning: Remove linen and waste first. Deal with the blood using the spill approach in “Managing spills of body fluid at work” before the terminal clean. Then clean from the cleanest area toward the dirtiest, using detergent before any disinfectant. Log the room, plus the spill.

workedExamples.situation: A colleague asks you to skip the bed rails so the room can be handed back sooner.
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline the shortcut. Bed rails are high-touch items inside the terminal clean. Tell the supervisor about the instruction and record that you cleaned the rails as the checklist requires.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves and an apron suited to the products in use
Detergent, and the disinfectant approved for the room under “Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals”
Colour-coded cloths and mops for the area
Terminal cleaning checklist for the room

commonErrors.error: Treating terminal cleaning as a longer routine clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the terminal checklist, which includes items that routine work does not reach.

commonErrors.error: Disinfecting a surface before it has been cleaned.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean with detergent first, then disinfect only where the schedule calls for it.

commonErrors.error: Wiping the surface dry before the product has had its contact time.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the surface wet for the product's contact time, then let it dry.
Clean every listed item on every occasion, because appearance does not reveal microbes.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Disinfectants are chemicals. Use the PPE on the product label and in “PPE for cleaning tasks: choosing, putting on and taking off”.
Where the patient was under added controls, follow “Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread” and the infection prevention team's instructions.
Product names, concentrations and contact times come from the product label and the site's approved list. None are given in this lesson.

qualityStandard: Every listed high-touch item is cleaned with detergent before any disinfectant is applied.
The room is reported as ready only after the terminal checklist is complete.
documentationEvidence: Terminal cleaning checklist signed for the room
Record of any item not cleaned, with the reason
summary: Terminal cleaning follows discharge and covers the immediate patient space together with the surrounding care area.
Clean high-touch items with detergent first, then disinfect only where the schedule calls for it.
Record the room and any gap, and never shorten the checklist.

knowledgeChecks.question: What separates a terminal clean from a routine clean?
options: It is triggered by discharge or transfer and also reaches the surrounding care area.
It is done only on weekends and only in the wards with no patients at all
It uses a different colour of cloth and nothing else and is done by a different team
It involves no detergent at all and the surfaces are only wiped with a dry cloth

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are high-touch items cleaned with detergent before disinfectant is applied?
options: Organic material can block the disinfectant from the surface, so the surface must be clean first.
Detergent is applied to a dry surface before any other step and is then wiped off with a cloth
Disinfectant works only on dry surfaces and must be left to dry naturally on the bed
The order matters less when the same cloth is used for both steps and the cloth is rinsed once a day

knowledgeChecks.question: A colleague asks you to skip the bed rails to finish sooner. What do you do?
options: Skip them if the bed looks clean and the staff member is in a hurry to leave the ward today
Clean them as the checklist lists, and tell the supervisor if the instruction conflicts with it.
Wipe the rails with a dry cloth only and then wipe them with the clean bed sheet
Leave the rails for the end-of-week deep clean and tell the patient they are clean

sourceReferences: Hospital Infection Prevention & Control Manual (Sri Lanka College of Microbiologists, 2021 copyright; uploaded 2022 file), section 4.6 Environmental cleaning and disinfection (types of cleaning: routine, terminal and scheduled); rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)

Cross-checked against HCG-04 (detergent first), HCG-06 and HCG-07 (discharge-level frequencies). Source priority: the Australian NHMRC guideline, as summarised in HCG-01 to HCG-20, governs where it conflicts with this source.
The same section gives product concentrations and dosing tables. These are not used, and product choice is left to HCG-08.
